'''John of Palermo''' ({{fl.|1221–1240}}) was a translator of mathematical works from [[Arabic]] to [[Latin]] who lived in [[Palermo]], Sicily. He worked in the court of [[Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor|Emperor Frederick II]]. 

John had been introduced into the court of Frederick II through the mathematician Domenico Ispano. John is mentioned by [[Leonardo Fibonacci]] in his ''[[The Book of Squares|Liber quadratorum]]'' (1225) and several problems from Arab texts by [[Omar Khayyam]] were posed to Fibonacci.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brown |first1=Ezra |last2=Brunson |first2=Jason C. |date=2008 |title=Fibonacci's Forgotten Number |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07468342.2008.11922284 |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |language=en |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=112–120 |doi=10.1080/07468342.2008.11922284 |s2cid=118986329 |issn=0746-8342|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Some court documents mention a Johannes de Panormo who is thought to be the same person. John translated an Arab [[manuscript]], possibly by [[Ibn al-Haytham]], on the parabola into Latin as the ''De duabus lineis semper approximantibus sibi invicem et nunquam concurrentibus''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Clagett |first=Marshall |date=1954 |title=A Medieval Latin Translation of a Short Arabic Tract on the Hyperbola |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/301678 |journal=Osiris |volume=11 |pages=359–385 |doi=10.1086/368586 |jstor=301678 |s2cid=143924428 |issn=0369-7827}}</ref> John as noted as a "notarius" and there are indications that Frederick was to send him to [[Tunis]] in 1240.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Greco |first=Pietro |date=2016 |title=Translations: How Europe discovered science |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s40329-016-0137-1 |journal=Lettera Matematica |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=105–110 |doi=10.1007/s40329-016-0137-1 |s2cid=163471469 |issn=2281-6917|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
